name: Pataleeswarar Temple, Thirupathiripuliyur (Cuddalore)
deity: Shiva as Pataleeswarar (Karaiyetreeswarar), with the Goddess Periyanayaki (Arundhava Nayaki)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, sung by Appar and Sambandar (7th century); Pallava and Chola periods
dynasty: Pallava and Chola, with later additions
summary: In the old heart of Cuddalore, under the patali tree, Shiva keeps the temple of Appar's homecoming — the Lord who, tradition says, brought the saint safely ashore when he was cast into the sea bound to a stone.

sections.history: Thirupathiripuliyur is the old temple quarter of Cuddalore, and its name gathers the shrine's story: the pathiri, or patali, the trumpet-flower tree sacred to the temple, and puliyur, the town of the tiger-footed sage Vyaghrapada. The temple of Shiva as Pataleeswarar is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the shrines of Nadu Nadu; both Appar and Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord. Tradition identifies the town with the Pataliputram of the Periya Puranam, where the young Appar lived for years as a Jain monk before he returned to the worship of Shiva — so that this temple is remembered as the place where he took up Shaivism once more. The shrine grew through the Pallava and Chola periods and is administered today by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is entered through a tall rajagopuram from the busy streets of the old town. Within the outer prakaram stands the Adi Pathiri, an ancient patali tree honoured as the sthala vriksham, the tree from which both the Lord and the town take their name. The Goddess Periyanayaki — called Arundhava Nayaki, she of rare penance — has her own shrine within the complex, and the story of Appar, woven through the temple's whole tradition, is never far from the worship here.
sections.legends: The great legend here is Appar's. After he left the Jain order, the Pallava king, urged by his opponents, ordered him bound to a stone pillar and cast into the sea. Appar sang the praise of the Namasivaya mantra, and the stone floated; tradition says it carried him ashore near Thirupathiripuliyur, where he came to worship the Lord who had saved him — and so Shiva here is also called Karaiyetreeswarar, the one who brought him to the shore. The sthala purana also tells that Vyaghrapada and Patanjali worshipped here, and that the Goddess performed penance beneath the patali tree.
sections.festivals: The annual brahmotsavam, with the Lord and the Goddess taken through the streets of the old town, is the temple's great festival. Maha Shivaratri, the monthly pradosham and the Shaiva observances of the year draw the town's devotees, and the saints of the Tevaram are honoured on their days; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: For all the bustle of Cuddalore around it, the temple keeps an old calm. Pilgrims stand before the Adi Pathiri tree, remember Appar, and sing his verse that begins 'Sotrunai vedhiyan' — the hymn tradition says he sang as the stone floated. Thirumanikuzhi and Thiruvahindrapuram are a short drive west along the Kedilam.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in Thirupathiripuliyur, the old town of Cuddalore, about half a kilometre from Tiruppadiripuliyur railway station on the Villupuram–Mayiladuthurai line. Cuddalore is well served by buses from Puducherry, about 25 km north, and from Chennai; Puducherry has the closest airport, and Chennai the nearest major international airport.
